prime.problem: Every later card is a page of equations. Without one move, multiplying rows against columns and reading the shapes, each equation looks new. With it, most of them turn out to be the same equation with different matrices.
prime.fits: The first card of the course. It sets the convention every card uses (rows are tokens, a layer is x · W) and the dot product that attention scores are built from.
expect: the dot product as agreement between two vectors
matrix multiply as a grid of dot products
the shape rule (m × n) · (n × p) → (m × p)
why matmul is nearly all the arithmetic at real width
prime.goal: Compute any entry of a matrix product in the tiny model by hand, predict any product's shape before computing it, and explain with measured numbers why wide models are almost all matmul.

attend: Why does the sign of Q row 2 · K row 1 (4.0013) tell you something about attention before any softmax runs?
In (m × n) · (n × p), which size disappears, and what happened to it inside each cell?
Why does a wrong transpose crash on Q · K but run silently on a · Wq?
At d = 4 matmuls are 44.6% of the work and at d = 896 they are 99.4%. Which term grows faster, and by what power of d?
Why does Qwen's count of multiply-adds per token land almost exactly on its parameter count?

must: multiply two vectors position by position and add → products are positive where the signs agree → big positive sum = vectors point the same way, negative = opposite → Q row 2 · K row 1 = 4.0013 is sat's best match, so attention scores are dot products

matrix product = one dot product per (row of A, column of B) → the shared inner size n is summed away in every cell → (m × n) · (n × p) → (m × p) → reading shapes predicts the output and catches mismatched inner sizes

rows are tokens and a layer is x · W with W (in, out) → T tokens in, T rows out → PyTorch's nn.Linear stores Wᵀ (out, in) → a non-square wrong transpose errors, but a square one (Wq, 4 × 4) runs silently and changes the loss 2.2067 → 2.1561

matmul on 3 × d with a d × d weight costs 3·d·d; norms, GELU and adds cost a few ops per number, about 3·d → matmul share rises with width: 44.6% at d = 4, 92.4% at d = 64, 99.4% at d = 896, 99.7% in Qwen2.5-0.5B → cost of a model ≈ its multiply-adds
elevated: About one multiply-add per weight per token: Qwen does 494,262,272 matmul multiply-adds per token against 494,032,768 parameters, so you can estimate a model's compute from its size
reference: tiny model: Q[0,0] = −1.0667, Q[0,1] = −0.0502, cosine of Q row 2 and K row 1 = 0.5992
tiny forward pass: 516 matmul multiply-adds, 642 other operations (rough count)
A @ B and A.matmul(B) are the same; K.T swaps rows and columns

compress.prompt: From memory, draw a (3 × 4) · (4 × 4) product: shade the row and column that make one cell, write the shape rule beside it, and add one sentence on why wider models are almost all matmul. Or explain it in 4 sentences.
checklist: a dot product multiplies matching positions and adds; its sign and size show agreement
each cell of A · B is one row of A dotted with one column of B
inner sizes must match and vanish; outer sizes give the result's shape
rows are tokens and layers are x · W with W (in, out); PyTorch stores Wᵀ
matmul cost grows like d², the rest like d, so width makes matmul dominate

retrieve.q: Explain in plain words what a dot product measures, using sat's query and cat's key as the example.
answer: positive products are positions where the signs agree
a large positive total means the two vectors point roughly the same way (cosine 0.5992)
so cat is the key that best matches sat's query

retrieve.q: Walk through how Q[0,0] = −1.0667 is computed, starting from the shapes.
answer: a is 3 × 4 and Wq is 4 × 4, so Q is 3 × 4
cell [0,0] uses row 0 of a and column 0 of Wq
sum −1.06667, which rounds to −1.0667

retrieve.q: You load a PyTorch nn.Linear weight into code that computes x @ W and forget to transpose it. When will you find out, and when won't you?
answer: nn.Linear stores (out, in); x @ W needs (in, out)
if in ≠ out the shapes don't match and matmul raises an error
if the matrix is square it runs and gives wrong numbers silently
in the tiny model, Wqᵀ instead of Wq moves the loss from 2.2067 to 2.1561 with no error

retrieve.q: A colleague says 'GELU and LayerNorm are expensive, optimise them first'. When are they right, and when is that wasted effort?
answer: by arithmetic, they matter only in very narrow models (44.6% matmul at d = 4)
at real width matmuls are 99.4–99.7% of the arithmetic
but arithmetic isn't time: element-wise steps are memory-bound and can take a real share of the seconds
so measure time before deciding, and expect matmul to dominate the operation count

compare.q: Both this card and the attention-scores card compute 4.0013. What does each card treat as the main idea, and what does attention add on top of the plain dot product?
answer: here 4.0013 is a dot product: a measure of how aligned two vectors are
attention computes all such pairs at once as Q · Kᵀ, a 3 × 3 matmul
it then divides by √d so the spread stays near 1, and masks the future
without √d the same dot products grow with width and saturate softmax

compare.q: An embedding lookup can be written as one-hot · E, a matmul. Why does the operation count here treat it as 0 multiply-adds, and what would it cost if you really multiplied?
answer: a one-hot row has a single 1, so the product just copies one row of E
real code indexes the row instead of multiplying, so it costs no arithmetic
multiplying would cost tokens × vocab × d: 3 × 5 × 4 = 60 in the tiny model, 7 × 151,936 × 896 in Qwen
the matmul view is useful for gradients, the lookup view for speed

predict.q: Make the tiny model's feed-forward hidden size 4 times wider instead of 2 (H = 16 instead of 8) and keep d = 4. Does the matmul share of the forward pass go up or down from 44.6%? Commit first.
predict.answer: Up only a little, from 44.6% to 45.2% (708 multiply-adds against 858 other operations). The two FFN matmuls double (96 → 192 each) but so does the GELU count (216 → 432), because GELU runs once per hidden number. Width d is what makes matmul dominate, since only matmul cost multiplies d by d. Check it by calling tiny_counts(H=16) in labs/vectors-and-matmul.py.

apply.task: Compute K[1,1] by hand: row 1 of a dotted with column 1 of Wk. a row 1 = [−1.0615, 0.6715, −0.8882, 1.2781]; Wk column 1 = [0.7, −0.2, −0.2, 0.3]. Then state the shape of K and how many multiply-adds the whole K = a · Wk takes.
apply.done: Products −0.74305, −0.13430, 0.17764, 0.38343; sum −0.31628, so K[1,1] = −0.3163, matching tiny.out. K is 3 × 4, and a · Wk takes 3 × 4 × 4 = 48 multiply-adds.
apply.hint: Keep 5 decimals in each product: a 4-decimal number times a 1-decimal weight is exact at 5.
